edits.english: “Until the ruling disseminates throughout the entire assembly of Israel” - This refers to those who convened to issue the ruling:

Rabbi Yonatan says: Even one hundred judges who sat in judgment to issue a ruling, and they deliberated on the matter and erred—they are not liable to bring an offering until all of them issue the ruling, as it is stated regarding the liability for the offering: “And if the entire assembly of Israel shall act unwittingly” (Leviticus 4:13). The term “entire” comes to emphasize: until all of them act unwittingly, meaning, until the ruling disseminates (is accepted) throughout the entire assembly of Israel, that this erroneous ruling is with the consent of “the entire assembly”—the Sanhedrin. Rav Huna, son of Rav Hoshaya, said: So too it is reasonable to conclude this, as throughout the entire Torah we maintain the principle that its majority is like its entirety, and here it does not say "assembly" alone, but rather it is written: “The entire assembly.” This is an additional emphasis. Since it is so, even if there are one hundred judges, all of them must issue the ruling.

A similar approach is found in the Yerushalmi, that one hundred judges who sat must all decide as one. There, it further raises a question: Is it enough that all of them decide to permit a prohibited matter, or must they decide based on one reason specifically? In the book B"Sh, a serious question was raised: How is it possible for one hundred to sit and judge? The Great Sanhedrin (which decides on such matters) consists of seventy-one members, and one does not add to them (as it is a scriptural decree, as God told Moses). So how can one hundred judge as a court? It remains unresolved. Some explained that the language is not precise, and it is merely an exaggeration, as there is no court of more than seventy-one (Chak Natan). Others wrote that perhaps it refers to a case where another central court was added to them (such as the court of twenty-three that sat at the entrance of the Temple, which was also a central court), and all of them judged the matter as one (Hora Gever). Others wrote that there were other important students worthy of issuing rulings before the court, who were also among those judging the matter (even if they do not count towards the quorum), and this is also how Rashi's language is interpreted (Zera Avraham). Indeed, some said that even though the Great Sanhedrin is not less than seventy-one, it was possible to add to it for various purposes (Meromei Sadeh), as we find in various places in the Talmud that the Men of the Great Assembly were one hundred and twenty elders who established halakhot for all of Israel (R. Tz. Chayot).
Rashi explains that 'until the ruling disseminates throughout the assembly of Israel' means in the session of the Sanhedrin, who are called 'assembly'.

If the court issued a ruling and one of them knew that they erred and told them that they were mistaken, even though those who permitted outnumbered the dissenters and the majority of the public acted according to their ruling—the court is exempt from an offering, and all those who acted are obligated to bring an individual sin-offering. This is in accordance with the words of Rabbi Yonatan (Rambam, Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 13:1).
For example, that one of them bowed his head - or a student, bowed his head, as it appeared that he agreed with their words, and the ruling was finalized.

One can infer from the language of the Mishna: This sage is liable, but if there was another who acted according to the court's ruling—he is exempt. And why? But indeed, the ruling was not finalized by all the judges, for we said that if not all the judges of the court issued the ruling, it is not called a ruling! And they answer: What are we dealing with here? For example, where that one of them who disagreed with them bowed his head and appeared to agree with them.

Come and hear proof from what we learned, which relates to this matter of Rabbi Yonatan: If the court issued a ruling, and one of them knew that they erred and said to them: "You are mistaken"—they are exempt. And we infer: The reason that they are exempt is specifically that he said to them: "You are mistaken." But if he was silent—they are liable, and the ruling is finalized. And why? But not all of them issued the ruling, and if so, this contradicts Rabbi Yonatan's words! They say in response: So too here, it is a case where that one bowed his head.

Rav Mesharshiyya raises an objection to the words of Rabbi Yonatan from what we learned: Our Sages relied on the words of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and on the words of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, who would say: One does not issue a decree upon the public unless the majority of the public can withstand it.

edits.hebrew: במארה אתם נארים וגו' - כגון שהגוי כולו דיכולין לקבלה. הכי משמע: אי איכא גוי כולו וקא עבר עליה האי גברא, אותי אתם קובעים. והכי כתוב בספרים במס' עבודת כוכבים בפ' אין מעמידין:

edits.english: “With the curse you are cursed, etc.” - for example, that the entire nation is able to accept it. This is what it means: if there is an entire nation and this person transgresses against it, “you rob Me.” And so it is written in the books in Tractate Avodah Zarah, in the chapter 'Ein Ma'amidin'.

And Rav Adda bar Abba said about this: What is the verse that teaches this? As it is stated: “With the curse you are cursed, yet you rob Me, the entire nation” (Malachi 3:9), for the entire nation accepted upon itself by oath (“with the curse”) the laws of tithes, and yet they transgressed them. But here it is written: “The entire nation,” and nevertheless, the majority is considered like the entirety, for from this verse our Sages relied that one does not issue a decree unless the majority of the public can withstand it. From this, there is a strong refutation of Rabbi Yonatan. And they agree: Indeed, it is a strong refutation, and his words are rejected.
If all of them are present - the Sanhedrin of seventy-one.
It is a ruling - even if not all of those who sat to issue the ruling actually issued it.

And they ask: If so, rather, now that Rabbi Yonatan's words, which were based on the superfluous word in the verse, have been refuted, what is the meaning of “the entire assembly” that the Merciful One states? What does this emphasis come to teach us? This is what it says: If all the judges are present and decide thus (according to the majority opinion)—it is a ruling, and if not all of them are present—it is not a ruling.

Regarding this matter of the judges' session, Rabbi Yehoshua says: When ten judges sit in judgment—the kolar (the chain of those going to be punished) is suspended around the neck of all of them. And they ask: Isn't this obvious? And they answer: This teaches us that even a student before his teacher, if he saw that an error was made and did not correct it—the obligation rests upon him, and he is not permitted to remain silent out of respect for the Rabbi.

It is related that Rav Huna, when he would go out to the court, would bring ten tanna'im of the study hall before him to be as if they were partners with him in judgment, for he would say: So that we will receive a splinter from the beam, meaning, that they would share the responsibility for the ruling with him. Similarly, it is related that Rav Ashi, when they would bring a tereifa before him to ask if the animal was a tereifa or not, would bring ten slaughterers from Mata Meḥasya and seat them before him. He said: So that we will receive a splinter from the beam.
